bodyMarkdown:
## Before you start

Percentages, especially repeated growth over several periods.

## The idea in plain language

If a business grows from 100 to 200 over four years, it did not grow 25 percent a year. Growth compounds, so each year's rise builds on a bigger base.

CAGR answers: what **steady** yearly rate would have produced this same journey? It is the smoothed-out rate, ignoring the bumps along the way.

## What is actually going on

Year-on-year growth compares consecutive periods and always divides by the earlier value.

CAGR looks only at the start and end, and asks what constant multiplier repeated over the period would connect them. Crucially, the exponent uses the number of **intervals**, not the number of data points: 2019 to 2023 is 4 years of growth, not 5.

Market share is a share of a total, so a company's share can fall while its absolute sales rise, if the market grew faster. Questions exploit exactly that.

## Every question type you will meet

Each of these is a shape a question in this topic actually comes in. Learn to recognise the shape first — in a timed paper, picking the right method is most of the battle, and the arithmetic is the easy part.

### 1. Year-on-year growth

**Spot it when:** 'growth rate in year X'.

1. Growth is (this year minus last year) divided by **last year**.
2. The denominator is always the earlier value.

**Worked through:** From 250 to 300 is $\dfrac{50}{250} = 20$ percent.

### 2. Compound annual growth rate

**Spot it when:** a start value, an end value, and a number of years.

1. CAGR is the single rate that would take you from start to end over that period.
2. Use $\left(\dfrac{\text{end}}{\text{start}}\right)^{1/n} - 1$.
3. Count the **intervals**, not the data points: 2019 to 2023 is four years, not five.

**Worked through:** Doubling over 3 years is a CAGR of $2^{1/3} - 1 \approx 26$ percent.

### 3. Comparing growth across entities

**Spot it when:** 'which grew fastest'.

1. Compare percentage growth, not absolute increase — a small base grows fast easily.
2. For multi-year comparisons use CAGR so the periods are comparable.

**Worked through:** A rise from 10 to 20 beats one from 500 to 600 in percentage terms, though it is far smaller in absolute terms.

## Check yourself

You are ready to start practising this topic when you can:

- Compute year-on-year growth with the right denominator.
- Compute and interpret a CAGR, counting intervals correctly.
- Explain why a small base flatters a growth rate.

workedExamples.stemMarkdown: Revenue rises from 120 to 210 between 2019 and 2023. Find the CAGR.
workedExamples.solutionMarkdown:
From 2019 to 2023 is 4 intervals, not 5.

$\text{CAGR} = \left(\dfrac{210}{120}\right)^{1/4} - 1$

$= (1.75)^{0.25} - 1 \approx 0.1503$, so about 15.03 percent per year.
workedExamples.altSolutionMarkdown: Sanity check: 15 percent compounded 4 times multiplies by roughly 1.75, matching 120 to 210.

formulaCards.title: Year-on-year growth
formulaCards.exampleMarkdown: From 175 to 210 is a 20 percent rise.

formulaCards.title: CAGR
formulaCards.bodyMarkdown: $\left(\dfrac{\text{End}}{\text{Start}}\right)^{1/n} - 1$, where $n$ is the number of intervals.

formulaCards.title: Market share
formulaCards.bodyMarkdown: $\dfrac{\text{company sales}}{\text{total market sales}} \times 100$. Share can fall while sales rise.
formulaCards.exampleMarkdown: Sales up from 50 to 60 while the market doubles from 200 to 500 means share fell from 25 to 12 percent.

commonTraps: Counting years instead of intervals. 2019 to 2023 is 4, not 5.
Averaging the yearly growth rates and calling it CAGR. Compounding is not additive.
Reading a falling market share as falling sales.
